label: DNS Client
description: Windows DNS Client resolver configuration, caching, NRPT policies, and DNS over HTTPS

l1: What Windows version and build number is the affected client running? (Get-ComputerInfo | Select OsName,OsVersion,OsBuildNumber)
Is this issue affecting one client, multiple clients on the same subnet, or clients across multiple sites?
What DNS server IPs are configured on the affected client — assigned via DHCP (option 6) or statically configured? (Get-DnsClientServerAddress)
Can the client reach the configured DNS server on UDP/TCP port 53? (Test-NetConnection <DNS IP> -Port 53)
Is the DNS Client service (Dnscache) running and set to Automatic? (Get-Service Dnscache | Select Name,Status,StartType)
Is the client domain-joined, Azure AD joined, Hybrid Azure AD joined, or a standalone workgroup machine? (Get-ComputerInfo | Select CsDomain,Workgroup)
Are all DNS names failing, or only specific namespaces — internal vs. external, short names vs. FQDNs, specific record types (A vs AAAA)?
When did the issue begin — Windows Update, GPO change, network reconfiguration, VPN client installation, or certificate expiry?
Does flushing the DNS resolver cache resolve the issue temporarily? (Clear-DnsClientCache or ipconfig /flushdns)
Is this a physical machine, Hyper-V VM, Azure VM, or VDI/Citrix session? (affects NIC virtualization and isolation)
Does the issue occur consistently or intermittently — if intermittent, does it correlate with network events (sleep/resume, DHCP lease renewal, VPN connect/disconnect)?
l2: Is the client using DHCP-assigned DNS or statically configured DNS — verify the correct DNS server is being assigned via DHCP option 6. (Get-NetIPConfiguration)
Are DNS suffix search lists configured via Group Policy (Computer or User) or locally — what is the search order? (Get-DnsClientGlobalSetting | Select SuffixSearchList)

Is DNS devolution enabled — what is the DevolutionLevel setting? Could devolution cause short names to resolve to the wrong domain suffix? (Get-DnsClientGlobalSetting | Select UseDevolution,DevolutionLevel)
Is the client configured to register DNS records dynamically — is dynamic update working, and are records appearing correctly in DNS? (Register-DnsClient, ipconfig /registerdns)
Is DNS over HTTPS (DoH) configured on this Windows 11 / Server 2022 client — what templates and encryption settings? (Get-DnsClientDohServerAddress)
Are Name Resolution Policy Table (NRPT) rules applied via GPO — do they affect the failing namespace or override the configured DNS server? (Get-DnsClientNrptPolicy, Get-DnsClientNrptRule)
If the client is on VPN — are the split-tunnel DNS settings correct? Is the VPN client injecting NRPT rules or overriding the primary DNS server? (Get-VpnConnection)
Is the DNS resolver cache holding stale negative cache entries (NXDOMAIN) for the failing name — what is the negative cache TTL? (Get-DnsClientCache | Where Status -ne Success)
Are third-party DNS agents, DNS filtering proxies, or endpoint security products intercepting or modifying DNS traffic on port 53? (Get-NetAdapterBinding)
Is IPv6 active — are AAAA queries failing while A record queries succeed, or vice versa? Is the client preferring IPv6 per RFC 6724? (Get-NetIPAddress, Get-NetRoute)
Is there a browser-level DoH configuration (Chrome, Edge) that bypasses the Windows DNS resolver entirely? (Check browser settings or Group Policy for DoH)
Is the client behind a captive portal or proxy that intercepts DNS before reaching the configured server? (Check network adapter proxy settings and detect captive portal via HTTP)
Are WMI filters or security filtering on GPOs preventing DNS-related Group Policy from applying? (gpresult /r)

l1: Run 'ipconfig /all' — share full output including DNS Servers, Connection-Specific DNS Suffix, DHCP Enabled, and IP address configuration.
Run 'nslookup <failing name>' — note the DNS server queried and the exact response (Timeout, Non-existent domain, Server failed, Refused, or wrong address).
Run 'nslookup <failing name> <explicit DNS IP>' — compare results with default DNS server vs. a known-good server (e.g., 8.8.8.8).
Run 'ping <failing hostname>' — does it fail at name resolution (could not find host) or at ICMP level (request timed out)?
Run 'Clear-DnsClientCache; ipconfig /registerdns' — flush cache and force registration, then retry and share results.
Run 'Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <failing name> -Port 80' — does it resolve the name and establish TCP connection?
Run 'Resolve-DnsName <failing name>' and 'Resolve-DnsName <failing name> -Server 8.8.8.8' — compare PowerShell outputs for internal vs. external DNS.
Is the issue specific to this client? Can another client on the same subnet resolve the same name? (isolates client vs. server issue)
l2: Run 'Get-DnsClientNrptPolicy' — are NRPT rules routing specific namespaces to different DNS servers or blocking resolution? (NRPT overrides default DNS server)
Run 'Get-DnsClient | Select InterfaceAlias,ConnectionSpecificSuffix,UseSuffixSearchList,RegisterThisConnectionsAddress' — verify per-adapter DNS settings.
Run 'Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4' and '-AddressFamily IPv6' — confirm per-interface DNS server assignments for dual-stack environments.
Run 'Get-DnsClientGlobalSetting' — review SuffixSearchList, UseDevolution, DevolutionLevel, QueryAdapterName, and SmartMultiHomedNameResolution.
Run 'Get-DnsClientCache | Where Status -ne "Success" | Select Name,Type,Status,TTL | Format-Table' — inspect failed or negative cache entries that may be causing false failures.
Run 'Get-DnsClientCache | Where Name -eq "<failing name>"' — is a stale or negative entry cached that needs to be cleared?

Capture DNS client ETL trace: 'netsh trace start capture=yes provider=Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Client level=5 keywords=0xFFFFFFFF tracefile=C:\dns_client.etl' — reproduce issue — 'netsh trace stop' — analyze with tracerpt.
Run 'gpresult /h C:\gpo_report.html' — open report and inspect Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Name Resolution Policy and DNS Client settings.
Run 'Get-NetIPConfiguration -Detailed' — review DNSServer, DNSSuffix, and InterfaceAlias for all adapters to identify configuration conflicts.
Run 'Resolve-DnsName <n> -DnsOnly -Type A' and 'Resolve-DnsName <n> -DnsOnly -Type AAAA' — compare IPv4 vs. IPv6 resolution to identify protocol-specific issues.
Run 'netsh winhttp show proxy' — proxy misconfiguration can affect DNS in browser and WinHTTP contexts; check for WPAD/DHCP option 252.
Run 'Get-DnsClientNrptRule' — list all NRPT rules including their namespace, DNS servers, DirectAccessDnsServers, and scope (GPO vs. local).

l1: Flush DNS resolver cache and re-register: 'Clear-DnsClientCache; ipconfig /registerdns' — retest immediately to eliminate stale cache as cause.
Restart the DNS Client service: 'Restart-Service Dnscache' — if service cannot restart, check dependent services (TCP/IP NetBIOS Helper, TCP/IP Protocol Driver).
Verify configured DNS server IPs are correct: 'Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4' — compare against expected domain DNS servers or DHCP option 6.
Test with an explicit public DNS server: 'Resolve-DnsName <name> -Server 8.8.8.8' — if this resolves but internal DNS does not, internal DNS server is the issue.
Restart the network adapter: 'Restart-NetAdapter -Name "<adapter>"' — this forces DHCP renewal and refreshes DNS settings from DHCP server.
Run 'gpupdate /force' if domain-joined — refresh Group Policy DNS settings including NRPT rules, suffix search lists, and DNS client settings.
Check if DNS Client service start type is correct: 'Set-Service Dnscache -StartupType Automatic' — should be Automatic or Automatic (Delayed Start).
l2: If NRPT rules are misdirecting queries: identify the offending rule via 'Get-DnsClientNrptRule' — remove via 'Remove-DnsClientNrptRule -Namespace <n>' or correct via Group Policy (Computer Config > Windows Settings > Name Resolution Policy).

If DoH is causing resolution failures on Windows 11: disable per-adapter via Settings > Network > DNS Server Assignment — or: 'Set-DnsClientDohServerAddress -ServerAddress <IP> -DohTemplate $null' to clear DoH configuration.
If stale negative caching persists: increase or remove the negative cache TTL on the authoritative DNS server (SOA Minimum TTL field) — on client, negative cache TTL is controlled by server SOA.

If VPN client is overriding DNS: check VPN client NRPT rules — 'Get-DnsClientNrptRule | Where Source -eq "DirectAccess"' — or review VPN client DNS configuration documentation; disable split DNS if not required.

If the client is registering wrong DNS records due to multiple NICs: adjust interface metrics — 'Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceAlias "<primary>" -InterfaceMetric 10' — set primary NIC to lower metric, then run 'ipconfig /registerdns'.

If AAAA queries cause failures and IPv6 is not needed: configure 'Prefer IPv4 over IPv6' via registry — HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters DisabledComponents = 0x20. Requires reboot. (Microsoft documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/networking/configure-ipv6-in-windows)

Analyze the DNS client ETL trace: use 'tracerpt C:\dns_client.etl -o C:\dns_report.evtx -of EVTX' — look for DNS_QUERY_REQUEST, DNS_QUERY_RESPONSE events and filter on failing name to identify RCODE and response time.

If browser DNS is bypassing Windows resolver: disable browser DoH in Group Policy (Chrome: DnsOverHttpsMode = off; Edge: same policy via Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Edge) — or via browser settings.

If DNS suffix search list is incorrect: configure via Group Policy (Computer Config > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client) or locally: 'Set-DnsClientGlobalSetting -SuffixSearchList @("domain1.com","domain2.com")'.

If Smart Multi-Homed Name Resolution is causing issues: disable via 'Set-DnsClientGlobalSetting -SmartMultiHomedNameResolution $false' — this feature queries all DNS servers on all adapters in parallel; disable if causing false failures.

l1: Run 'ipconfig /all > C:\ipconfig_client.txt' — capture complete IP configuration including DNS servers and connection-specific suffixes.
Run 'nslookup <failing name> > C:\nslookup_default.txt' and 'nslookup <failing name> <DNS IP> > C:\nslookup_explicit.txt' — document failure mode with default vs. explicit DNS server.
Run 'Get-DnsClientCache | Out-File C:\dns_cache.txt' — capture current resolver cache including stale and negative entries.
Export Application event log: 'wevtutil epl Application C:\App_Events.evtx' — contains DNS Client service events and application-level resolution failures.
l2: Capture DNS client ETL trace: 'netsh trace start capture=yes provider=Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Client level=5 keywords=0xFFFFFFFF tracefile=C:\dns_client_trace.etl' — reproduce issue — 'netsh trace stop' — analyze with tracerpt.
Run 'gpresult /h C:\gpo_dns_report.html' — comprehensive Group Policy report showing applied DNS-related policies including NRPT and suffix search lists.
Run 'Get-DnsClientNrptPolicy | Out-File C:\nrpt_policy.txt' — export NRPT policy configuration showing namespace routing rules.
Run 'Get-DnsClientGlobalSetting | Out-File C:\dns_global.txt' — export global DNS client settings including devolution, suffix search list, and smart multi-homed resolution.
Run 'Get-DnsClientServerAddress | Out-File C:\dns_server_addresses.txt' — export per-interface DNS server assignments for IPv4 and IPv6.
Run 'Get-NetIPConfiguration -Detailed | Out-File C:\net_ip_config_detailed.txt' — capture detailed network configuration for all adapters.
Export System event log: 'wevtutil epl System C:\System_Events.evtx' — contains DNS Client service startup and system-level events.
TSS full data collection: '.\TSS.ps1 -Scenario NET_DNScli' — run on the affected client, reproduce the issue, stop when prompted — collects comprehensive logs for Microsoft Support analysis.

client_not_resolving.title: Client cannot resolve any DNS names
client_not_resolving.description: Complete DNS resolution failure on client - no names resolve from default DNS server

steps.expect: Status: Running, StartType: Automatic — DNS Client service must be operational
DNS Servers field shows valid IPs — not blank, not 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1 (unless self-hosting DNS)
TcpTestSucceeded: True — confirms DNS server is reachable on network
If resolves with explicit IP but not default, DNS client configuration or cache is the issue
If resolves via public DNS, internal DNS server is the problem; if fails with both, client-side issue
Check for NRPT rules routing queries to a wrong or unreachable DNS server
Cache cleared and DNS records re-registered — retest immediately
DNS Client service restarts cleanly — verify with Get-Service
Refreshes NRPT rules and DNS suffix search list from Group Policy — may require reboot for GPO changes
Resolves correctly using default DNS server with reasonable response time
Name resolves to correct IP and ICMP succeeds (if not blocked by firewall)

nrpt_misdirecting.title: NRPT rules misdirecting DNS queries
nrpt_misdirecting.description: Name Resolution Policy Table rules routing queries to incorrect DNS servers

steps.expect: Lists active NRPT rules — check if any namespace matches the failing name
Shows source of each rule (GPO, DirectAccess, manual) and target DNS server addresses
If fails here, NRPT is routing to a broken or unreachable DNS server

steps.action: gpresult /h C:\gpo_report.html — open and check Name Resolution Policy section
steps.expect: Identify which GPO is pushing the offending NRPT rule — check security filtering and WMI filters
Rule removed immediately — test resolution

steps.action: If GPO-pushed: edit in GPMC — Computer Config > Windows Settings > Name Resolution Policy — remove or correct rule — gpupdate /force
steps.expect: Offending rule removed from client after GPO refresh
Offending rule no longer present in NRPT table
Resolves correctly via default DNS server

ipv6_resolution_failing.title: IPv6 (AAAA) resolution failing while IPv4 works
ipv6_resolution_failing.description: Client cannot resolve AAAA records but A records resolve successfully

steps.expect: Returns IPv4 address successfully
Fails with timeout or NXDOMAIN — confirms IPv6-specific issue
Check if client has valid IPv6 address — if no IPv6, AAAA queries may fail due to lack of source address
Check if IPv6 DNS servers are configured — if blank, AAAA queries may not be sent

steps.action: If IPv6 not needed: Disable IPv6 on adapter via Set-NetAdapterBinding -Name '<adapter>' -ComponentID ms_tcpip6 -Enabled $false
steps.expect: IPv6 disabled — client will only query A records

steps.action: If IPv6 needed: Configure IPv6 DNS servers via DHCPv6 or static assignment
steps.expect: IPv6 DNS servers configured — AAAA queries will succeed
Returns IPv6 address successfully
